introduction: This guide is about love inside a community: what the friends of God owe one another. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes believers in Persia who walked into each other’s houses as their own, asks that each regard the other as master, that quarrels be mended within a day, that shortcomings go unmentioned, and that no discord of views be allowed to take root. A hundred of the guide’s three hundred quotations are given here, ten from each tenth of its length. Beside them stand a hundred voices from elsewhere: the first church in Acts, Paul’s letters to quarrelling congregations, the Qur’an on counsel and on the cable of God, Proverbs, Aristotle, Bacon and Montaigne on friendship. About one in four raises a difficulty and ends in a question. Aristotle doubts that goods held in common are cared for, Gibran wants space between the pillars, Milton and Mill defend the clash of opinions, Locke denies that anyone can be compelled into unity, and Jesus kept company the Psalmist would have avoided.
questions: The Persian friends shared houses, food and clothes until it “became a hindrance in the conduct of material affairs”. Read Acts, Aristotle and Gibran beside this. How close should a community’s members be?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá never mentioned individual shortcomings and asks the friends to do likewise; Jesus says to tell a brother his fault privately. How do you decide between silence and speaking?
“Discord of views is more severe than deadly poison.” Milton, Mill and Jefferson prize difference of opinion. What is the line between a variety of views and a discord of them, and who draws it?
Consultation is to be held in “the utmost love, harmony and sincerity”. What happens to sincerity when harmony is the stronger wish, and what has helped groups you know keep both?

“Treasure the companionship of the righteous and eschew all fellowship with the ungodly.” Jesus was called a friend of publicans and sinners. Whose company strengthens you, and whose do you owe your own?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says America had not yet reached the love of the believers in the East. What would have to change for a community you know to be described as he describes the friends in Persia?

outside.why: The friends must “ever be ready and willing to sacrifice their own lives for each other”. Jesus: greater love hath no man than this.
One believer meeting another should be “as though … a lover has met his true beloved”. The Bible’s pattern of such a friendship: the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that every believer be to every other as a lover to the beloved. Montaigne could give only one reason for the one great friendship of his life: because it was he, because it was I. Can that kind of love be asked of a whole community?
“A soul independent of all the other souls … cannot live for the twinkling of an eye.” Donne: no man is an island, entire of itself.
“Of all pilgrimages the greatest is to relieve the sorrow-laden heart.” Isaiah on the fast God has chosen: to undo the heavy burdens, and to deal thy bread to the hungry.
The Persian friends opened each other’s provision boxes and wore each other’s clothes. The first church in Jerusalem: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own.

This brotherhood, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá admits, “really became a hindrance in the conduct of material affairs”. Aristotle thought that inevitable: what is common to the greatest number has the least care bestowed upon it. How much of mine and thine does love need to leave standing?

“There was no duality but complete mutuality.” Gibran’s counsel to those who love: stand together yet not too near together, for the pillars of the temple stand apart. Is there a closeness that weakens a fellowship?
“You must be ready to sacrifice your possessions in another’s behalf.” The Qur’an praises those of Medina who preferred the emigrants above themselves, though poverty was their own lot.
If a friend arrived ill, they would care for him; if sad, comfort him. Paul: bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
When a friend arrived in their city, all would rejoice and gather to meet him. Peter’s rule for the same occasion: use hospitality one to another without grudging.
“An Oriental sacrificeth his life for an Occidental! What attraction, what love, what relationship is this!” Ruth the Moabite to an Israelite: where thou diest, will I die.
The friends are to become “the lowliest servants to one another”. Jesus, having washed his disciples’ feet: ye also ought to wash one another’s feet.
To serve the Cause is “to build the bonds of love”, with meekness and humility. Jesus: whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant.
“Let each consider the other his master.” Paul: in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.

The friends are to be “proud in humility and submissiveness to each other”. Emerson told his countrymen to trust themselves and take themselves for their portion. What is the difference between humility towards a friend and the loss of one’s own voice?
“Lead them to … meekness and obedience, and to the service of one another.” Paul: by love serve one another; but if ye bite and devour one another, take heed.
“The principle of consultation is one of the most fundamental elements of the divine edifice.” Proverbs: in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Even in ordinary affairs people should consult. The Qur’an counts among the faithful those whose affairs are a matter of counsel.

Those who consult must behave “in the utmost love, harmony and sincerity”. Mill adds what consultation is for: he who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that. Can harmony and frank disagreement be had in the same room?
“Ye should first consult together, and thereafter devise a plan”, and confirmations will follow. The first council of the church reported its decision so: it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us.
The Assemblies of Chicago, New York and Washington are to come together, as the West with the East. Kipling’s ballad on when East and West do meet.
“That dust will settle and that discord will disappear.” Blake on what makes the difference between wrath that ends and wrath that grows: whether it is told.
Never “allow any trace of past grievances to cross their minds”. Proverbs: he that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.
“Even if one or two days pass with an unresolved difference, it will become firmly rooted.” Paul gives less time: let not the sun go down upon your wrath.
When a disagreement clouds two friends, others must act quickly. Jesus puts reconciliation before worship: leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way.
“I have not called attention to any of your individual shortcomings.” Jesus: why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá suggests the friends pass over one another’s shortcomings in silence. Jesus also says: if thy brother trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone. When is silence the loving course, and when is speaking?
“The very unity of the friends of God hath been and shall ever be the cause of guiding mankind.” Jesus: by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
“If this matter is not achieved, nothing is achieved.” Paul on every gift without charity: I am nothing.
To reconcile the loved ones “is the greatest of all deeds in the sight of” God. Jesus: blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God.

This gathering is bound by nothing “racial, patriotic, family, commercial … or political”. Tocqueville marvelled that Americans form associations for every purpose. What can a bond without interests do that those cannot, and where is it weaker?

“Bodily relationships may pass … but the spiritual relationship is eternal.” Jesus, told that his mother and brothers were outside: whosoever shall do the will of my Father, the same is my brother, and sister.

The spiritual tie is ranked above the tie of blood. Mencius thought any teaching that loosened the claims of family struck at the root of virtue. What is owed to kin that is not owed to fellow-believers, and the other way about?
The friends are to rise “with one accord” until they are “as one being and one soul”. Acts begins the church’s story the same way: they were all with one accord in one place.
Where people gather to speak of God, the Spirit “will blow gently over them”. The Qur’an: there is no secret conference of three but He is their fourth.
“If a small number of people gather lovingly together … that gathering will exert its influence over all the earth.” Jesus: where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I.
A small band, at one in their fellowship. Henry V makes a band of brothers out of a few soldiers before a battle. What makes a few people into a company, and does it need an enemy?
Gatherings exist “to keep them alert, vigilant, loving”. Hebrews: not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, but exhorting one another.

Attendance at gatherings keeps the friends awake and loving. Seneca says he comes home from a crowd more greedy, more cruel and less human. What distinguishes a gathering that improves people from one that does not?
Assemblies filled with love become “a guiding constellation” for mankind. The Great Law of the Haudenosaunee pictures a tree of peace whose roots spread in four directions for any nation to follow.

“Peace must first be established among individuals, until it leadeth in the end to peace among nations.” The Confucian Great Learning sets out the same widening: persons, families, states, the whole kingdom.
Peace begins between persons. UNESCO’s founders in 1945: since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá builds peace upward from love between individuals. Kant looked instead to law and the balance of states, and expected little from goodwill. Which has kept more peace: affection, or institutions that do not depend on it?
“They should have among them but one heart and soul.” Jesus’ prayer for those who would believe: that they all may be one.
“What fault can be found in these things?” Jesus asked his accusers the same: many good works have I shewed you; for which of those works do ye stone me?
“Strive to become … the lamps of divine guidance shining amongst the kindreds of the earth.” Jesus: ye are the light of the world.
“Did God create us for love or for enmity? … Surely He has created us for love.” Mencius: human nature tends to good as water tends to flow down.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá answers his own question without hesitation: we were created for love. Kant: out of such crooked material as man is made of, nothing can be hammered quite straight. What would each say to the other’s evidence?
“We must prove ourselves Bahá’ís in reality, and not merely in words.” Jesus’ test for anyone who claims to speak for God: by their fruits ye shall know them.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá prays “that every stranger may become a friend … every outsider become an intimate”. Hebrews: be not forgetful to entertain strangers.
“The honor and virtue of that home consists in its unity and harmony”; so with a village, a nation. Lincoln: a house divided against itself cannot stand.
“Treasure the companionship of the righteous and eschew all fellowship with the ungodly.” The first verse of the Psalter says the same.
Fellowship with the righteous quickens the heart. Proverbs: he that walketh with wise men shall be wise.
Bahá’u’lláh counsels avoiding the company of the ungodly. Jesus was reproached for keeping it: a friend of publicans and sinners. Whose company is a person strong enough to keep?
The seeker should treasure those who have renounced the world and avoid “boastful and worldly people”. Thoreau’s reason for going to the woods: the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
God is best praised by loving His loved ones and protecting them “that none may any longer oppress them”. Proverbs: open thy mouth for the dumb; plead the cause of the poor and needy.
“Regard the people of the world as dead and seek the fellowship of the living.” Jesus used the same hard figure: let the dead bury their dead.

Those who have not breathed this fragrance are “accounted among the dead”. Terence’s character holds that nothing human is foreign to him. How does one keep a figure of speech like this from becoming contempt?
“Be united, stand ye together.” Aesop’s father with the bundle of sticks: singly they snap; bound, they cannot be broken.
The friends are to cleave to the Covenant so that hatred and error may be dispelled. Paul: endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
“Wherefore fear ye, O My well-beloved ones? Who is it that can dismay you?” The Psalm: the Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá “completely forgot” a persecutor’s wrongs and had the friends honour him. Jesus on the cross: Father, forgive them.
All must be guided, “nay, compelled”, to gather under the Word of Unity. The word is from a parable: compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes of compelling the friends to unity. Locke argued that no one can be compelled in matters of the soul, since faith forced is not faith. What kind of compelling could a community of love use?
Some aim “to create division in the Cause of God and destroy the unity of the Bahá’ís”. Paul to Rome: mark them which cause divisions and offences, and avoid them.
Division made from within is the harder kind. The Psalmist: it was not an enemy that reproached me; it was thou, mine acquaintance.
“Disunity is tantamount to death and destruction, whilst harmony conferreth life.” Jesus: every city or house divided against itself shall not stand.
“Differ not among yourselves, lest the hearts of the deniers rejoice.” The Qur’an: dispute not one with another lest ye falter and your strength depart from you.
“Beware lest ye differ in the Cause — gather ye on the shore of this Most Great Sea.” The Qur’an: hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of God, and do not separate.
Friendship is “an ornament for the temple of man … a crown for his head and a light for his countenance”. Proverbs: ointment and perfume rejoice the heart; so doth the sweetness of a man’s friend.
An ornament, a crown, a light. Aristotle: without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods.
The more the bonds of love increase, “the more it brings joy to soul and conscience”. Bacon on what a friend does: it redoubleth joys, and cutteth griefs in halves.

“Discord of views is more severe than deadly poison.” Milton: where there is much desire to learn, there of necessity will be much arguing, many opinions; for opinion in good men is but knowledge in the making. What is the difference between a discord of views and a variety of them?
The friends are to prevent discord of views. Jefferson, after a bitter election: every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle. How does a community tell the two apart?

Differing views are called a blow that could efface the Cause. Mill held that if all mankind minus one were of one opinion, they would have no right to silence the one. What does a community lose when it prizes agreement?
Discord of views must be prevented. Paul to Corinth: that ye all speak the same thing, and be perfectly joined together in the same mind.
“Be ye … united … lest ye be tempted to divide and thy strength vanisheth.” The Preacher: a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
A minister offers his church for Bahá’í meetings, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá welcomes it. Jesus, of a stranger doing good in his name: he that is not against us is on our part.
The letter “bore testimony to the unity and harmony among the friends”. The Psalm: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
“Become as united as the stars of the Pleiades.” Job is asked whether he can bind the sweet influences of that cluster; the image of stars held together is very old.
The friends must love each other so sincerely “as to move the hearts of those who come in touch with them”. Tertullian reports the pagans of Carthage so moved: see how they love one another.

May this gathering not be like those “who forget each other as soon as they disperse”. James has a figure for it: a man who looks at his face in a glass and straightway forgets what manner of man he was. What makes a meeting last past its ending?
If someone wishes to separate from the flock, persuade and encourage him “so that this secluded sheep may return”. Jesus’ shepherd leaves the ninety and nine and goes after the one.
“There is no mightier bond in the world of being than the attachment of the heart.” The Song of Solomon: love is strong as death.
“America has not yet reached this station … they must grow in love for each other.” The letter to Ephesus in Revelation: I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love.
“How sweet is this moment when I am engaged in remembering you.” Paul: I thank my God upon every remembrance of you.
From the love of the friends ‘Abdu’l-Bahá is “like a surging sea”. Shakespeare’s sonnet: if the while I think on thee, dear friend, all losses are restored.
His heart has no attachment “save the countenance of the friends”. Paul to the Thessalonians: ye are our glory and joy.
“Be thou a sincere friend and a loving companion unto all.” Emerson’s definition: a friend is a person with whom I may be sincere; before him I may think aloud.
A sincere friend “unto all”. Aristotle: one cannot be a friend to many people in the perfect sense. What is kept, and what is given up, when friendship is widened to everyone?
When ‘Abdu’l-Bahá hears that the friends are in harmony, “my health improves more and more”. The elder in John’s letter: I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth.

“Letters have been and are half of meeting.” John closes a letter wishing for the other half: I will not with ink and pen write unto thee; I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face. What does a letter carry, and what does it leave behind?
“The world of love requires at all times the mention and praise of the loved ones.” Paul: in honour preferring one another.
A sense of their own powerlessness is what gathers them round the Cause. Paul was told: my strength is made perfect in weakness.
“Teach them to recognize the poverty of their own nature.” Bunyan’s shepherd boy: he that is down needs fear no fall; he that is low, no pride.
“Assemble Thy loved ones beneath the shadow of the tree of Thy oneness.” Isaiah: he shall gather together the dispersed from the four corners of the earth.
“The Day is approaching when God shall bring the faithful together.” Jesus: other sheep I have; there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
Those who “consign their own selves to oblivion” attain real union. Jesus: whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it.
Union “in the world that dieth not”. Shelley: the One remains, the many change and pass. Is the union hoped for here a union of persons who remain themselves?
